How to cancel or transfer electricity, gas and other services after a death (Australia)

By the Afterkeep research team · Reviewed on 9 Nov 2026

Contact each provider named on the bills (electricity, gas, water, phone, internet). Energy retailers can put the account into the "Estate of", transfer it to a joint holder or new occupant, keep temporary supply on, or close it and send a final bill to the estate. You usually need a certified death certificate and the account details. The free Australian Death Notification Service can notify many participating banks, telcos and utilities at once once the death is registered.

Key facts

  • Contact each retailer; details are on the bill
  • Options: transfer, "Estate of", temporary supply or close
  • Usually needs a certified death certificate
  • ADNS notifies many providers at once

What are the steps?

  1. Find the providers: the retailer's contact details are on each bill. Redirected mail and bank statements help you spot accounts.
  2. Once a death certificate has been issued by the state or territory registry, use the free Australian Death Notification Service to notify participating banks, phone and internet providers and utility companies in one go. They contact you within 10 working days.
  3. Call energy retailers directly too. Decide whether anyone still needs power or gas at the property.
  4. AGL customers: AGL says the easiest way to tell it is its NotifyNOW online platform (run by bereavement specialists Phillips & Cohen Associates, which can also notify other registered companies), or chat or phone. It asks for your details and relationship, the executor's details, the account details and what to do with the service.
  5. Keeping supply on: a joint account holder can usually have the account moved into their name, or a new occupant can open a new account. ENGIE and Ergon both describe this.
  6. Leaving the property empty for now: ask for the account to be kept as the "Estate of" or for temporary supply. Ergon says this needs the death certificate and a letter from the executor or administrator.
  7. Supply no longer needed: ask the retailer to close the account (and disconnect supply if appropriate) and send the final bill to the estate.
  8. Have ready: the deceased's full name, address, date of birth and date of death, the account number, and the executor's or solicitor's details.
  9. Stuck? Each state and territory has a free energy (and in most states water) ombudsman scheme; the AER lists them all.

Frequently asked questions

Who can close or transfer a deceased person's energy account?

Usually the executor or next of kin. ENGIE, for example, accepts a primary or joint account holder, the executor, the deceased's solicitor, or a trustee or business partner.

Will the power be cut off when the account holder dies?

Not automatically. Retailers can keep supply on under the "Estate of", transfer the account, or arrange temporary supply until the property is sorted.

How do I close a deceased person's AGL account?

Tell AGL through its NotifyNOW online platform, or by chat or phone. Have your name and contact details, your relationship to the account holder, the executor's name and details, the deceased's account details and what you want done. If supply stays on, Phillips & Cohen Associates manages the process; for a transfer AGL contacts the new account holder; closing the account triggers a final bill.

What documents do I need?

NSW Government guidance says you'll usually need a certified copy of the death certificate and the account details, plus proof of identity to transfer a service into your name. Some retailers also ask for an executor's letter.

What is the Australian Death Notification Service?

A free online service that lets you tell multiple participating organisations (banks, telcos, utilities and others) about a death in a single notification, after the death has been registered. Organisations then contact you within 10 working days.

Who pays the final energy bill?

Retailers send the final bill to the estate. Talk to the executor before paying it personally.
